Word-initial vowel — does the lead-in fix it?

You heard avoka as voka. The initial a was never missing from the crop — it is there in the alignment, 5 frames of it. What is missing is its acoustic onset, which the model realises earlier, in the frames belonging to the preceding space. Measured across the carrier, the eight frames before the cut carry 1.8× to 13× the energy of the eight after it. Cutting exactly on the token boundary therefore shears off the vowel attack.

lead=2 extends the cut back by two token slots — the blank and the space, i.e. the transition — without reaching the previous word's final vowel, which sits one slot further back and would make it sound like i-avoka.
All three models, as asked. torch is the 1.11 GB checkpoint, fp32 the 141.8 MB export, fp16 the 72 MB one. torch and fp32 are sample-identical (corr 1.00000000 on every word), so if they ever differ by ear, something is wrong with the measurement rather than the models. fp16 sits at 0.9988–0.99998.
